editorial.summary: At forty-eight, David revives Thumbs Up in Los Angeles without Critter or Harry and deliberately reframes driving his mother's Lexus from pathetic to cool. A brief Hollywood Boulevard encounter turns a private visitor's appreciative attitude into a prompt for David. After a weapons/surplus and wig-shopping montage, he returns to the Hollywood Sign area, abandons an unsatisfying landmark painting, paints fruit vendor Annie, trades it for coconut juice, then collaborates and trades drawings with Javier. The ending explicitly redefines Thumbs Up: not necessarily hitchhiking, but leaving the house, meeting people, changing perspective and making oneself happy. This is new self-reflective Los Angeles material, not merely a retrospective montage. Every idea remains in the source layer; private people, family histories, addresses, legal questions, lyrics and speaker identities remain bounded.

connections.why: David explicitly restarts the format in Los Angeles rather than merely describing the old series.
The mother's-Lexus line stages aging and dependence as either shame or continued play.
David speaks both pathetic and cool versions, then consciously chooses the latter.
He contrasts filming at twenty-eight with the present return twenty years later.
Critter and Harry are named as absent because they have other lives, not silently erased.
A private visitor recognizes David, but the useful takeaway becomes the visitor's appreciation rather than fandom.
The visitor's phrase becomes David's behavioral prompt for the rest of the episode.
Weapons, badge, armor and wigs become a comic montage without proving purchases or legality.
David repeatedly returns to the Hollywood Sign after disliking his first composition.
Dissatisfaction is retained as the cause of a compositional change, not edited away.
Crop and angle are observable painting decisions before they become a life metaphor.
Signing early is explicitly attributed to insecurity rather than packaged as mystique.
The fruit vendor replaces the Hollywood Sign as the painting's subject.
A painting is exchanged for coconut juice, echoing earlier Thumbs Up exchanges without implying a market valuation.
David breaks his own anti-collaboration advice after Javier begins drawing.
Coconut juice is used or discussed as paint medium, but the archive must not turn the joke into conservation advice.
A provocative parenting question does not establish Javier's family or abuse history.
David says the format is about leaving the house and connecting, not only hitchhiking.
